explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, writes, “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD…” Shaving a few crumbs off every sale might feel tiny, but the verse doesn't treat it that way. He's serious about honest dealing.

explanations.answer: As a small thing He overlooks
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, because a rigged scale can look like a tiny trick. But the verse uses the word abomination, and nobody picks that word for a small thing. Solomon says dishonest scales are “an abomination to the LORD…” so He is not shrugging at them.

Solomon never tells the buyer to just watch the scale harder. The verse says, “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD…” The scale itself is what He is talking about. Honesty in the weighing matters to Him.
Yes! The second half of the verse says, “…but an accurate weight is His delight.” Same scale, same counter, and a whole different reaction from the LORD. An honest weight makes Him glad.

Not quite. The warning side is the dishonest scale from the first half of the verse. The flip side is the honest one, and the verse says, “…but an accurate weight is His delight.” Accurate weight brings delight, not a warning.
I can see why a careful weight might feel like a lot of work. But the verse never calls it a burden. It says, “…but an accurate weight is His delight.” The LORD is pleased by it.

Right on. The proverb says, “When pride comes, disgrace follows…” Pride walks in first and disgrace shows up right behind it, no invitation needed. I've learned that a puffed-up chest and a quick fall go together.
Pride is sure applause is coming, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “When pride comes, disgrace follows…” The crowd never gets the chance to clap. Disgrace shows up instead.
Money is not what follows pride in this verse. Solomon says, “When pride comes, disgrace follows…” Wealth isn't mentioned at all. Disgrace is the one trailing behind.
Yep, that's the verse. Solomon says, “…but with humility comes wisdom.” Pride gets disgrace, and humility gets wisdom. I'd say that's a pretty good trade.
It's actually true. The verse says, “…but with humility comes wisdom.” Solomon puts it right beside the line about pride and disgrace, so the two halves answer each other.
That's the one. The verse says, “The integrity of the upright guides them…” It's like an inner compass that doesn't need batteries. The upright follow what's honest and whole in them.
Riches don't get the steering wheel here. Solomon says, “The integrity of the upright guides them…” He'll get to money in the next verse, and it doesn't go well for riches.

Reputation is how people see you, and the verse is about something deeper. It says, “The integrity of the upright guides them…” What guides them is their integrity itself, not what others say about them.

You've got it, baker. The verse says, “…but the perversity of the faithless destroys them.” Integrity guides the upright, and perversity wrecks the faithless. They're taken down by their own twisted ways.
Poverty isn't in this verse at all. Solomon says, “…but the perversity of the faithless destroys them.” Their own crooked ways are what bring them down.
That'd make a good drama, but the verse doesn't say it. Solomon says, “…but the perversity of the faithless destroys them.” No rival has to lift a finger, because their own crooked ways do the job.
Right! The verse says, “…but righteousness brings deliverance from death.” The first half says riches are worthless in the day of wrath. So money can't buy a way out, but righteousness brings one.
Hard work is good, but it's not what this verse names. Solomon says, “…but righteousness brings deliverance from death.” Labor isn't mentioned.
Strength doesn't carry anyone out in this chapter. Verse 7 says the hope of the wicked man's strength vanishes. And verse 4 says, “…but righteousness brings deliverance from death.”
That's not what the verse says. Solomon says, “…but the wicked fall by their own wickedness.” Nobody sneaks up and sticks out a foot. The fall comes from their own wickedness.
Right, it's false. The verse says, “…but the wicked fall by their own wickedness.” No one else trips them up. It's their own wickedness that brings them down.
That's the word. The verse says, “…but the faithless are trapped by their own desires.” They chase what they want, and it closes around them like a trap. Their own desires are the cage.
Neighbors don't set the trap here. Solomon says, “…but the faithless are trapped by their own desires.” The snare comes from what they want themselves.
Promises sound close, since the word is faithless, but the verse doesn't say it. Solomon says, “…but the faithless are trapped by their own desires.” What traps them is what they crave.

Close, but the verse splits them up. It says, “The righteous man is delivered from trouble; in his place the wicked man goes in.” Only the righteous man gets delivered, and the wicked man goes in where he was.
Yes, it's false. Solomon says, “The righteous man is delivered from trouble; in his place the wicked man goes in.” The righteous man is delivered, and the wicked man takes his place in the trouble.
Right. The verse says, “…but through knowledge the righteous are rescued.” The ungodly man uses his mouth to tear a neighbor down. The righteous are rescued through knowledge.
Courage is a good thing, but the verse names something else. Solomon says, “…but through knowledge the righteous are rescued.” Knowledge is the rescue.
Good friends are a gift, but this verse doesn't mention them. It says, “…but through knowledge the righteous are rescued.” Knowledge is what rescues them.
Yes! The verse says, “By the blessing of the upright a city is built up…” The wicked tear a city down with their mouths, and the upright build it up with a blessing. Words can do either one.
Walls sound sensible, but the verse points at people. Solomon says, “By the blessing of the upright a city is built up…” What lifts the city is the blessing of the upright.
The king's treasury isn't what the verse names. It says, “By the blessing of the upright a city is built up…” The upright, not the king's money, are what build up the city.

That's true. The verse ends, “…but a man of understanding remains silent.” It sits right next to the line about showing contempt for a neighbor, which Solomon says lacks judgment. Sometimes the wise move is a closed mouth.
It's true. Solomon says, “…but a man of understanding remains silent.” The first half says whoever shows contempt for his neighbor lacks judgment. So a man of understanding stays quiet.
That's the one. The verse says, “A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.” A secret handed to a trustworthy person stays safe. A gossip hands it to the next person.
Keeping your distance can be handy, but it isn't what the verse says. Solomon says, “…but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.” What the trustworthy person keeps is the secret someone shared.

A record sounds like someone writing it all down, and that's the opposite of the idea. The verse says, “…but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.” A trustworthy person holds on to what was trusted to them.
Right on. The verse says, “…but with many counselors comes deliverance.” A nation with no guidance falls, and a nation with plenty of counselors is delivered. More good voices help it stand.
An army isn't what Solomon names. He says, “…but with many counselors comes deliverance.” What brings deliverance is guidance, not soldiers.
One strong king is not the answer in this verse. Solomon says, “…but with many counselors comes deliverance.” The word is many, not one.
That's right. The verse says, “…but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” Putting up security for a stranger leads to suffering. Staying out of debt leads to security.
Staying out of debt is not a lonely road in this verse. Solomon says, “…but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” Security is what he gets.
Watchful sounds sensible, but it isn't the word. Solomon says, “…but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” Secure is what he is.
That's it. The verse says, “A gracious woman attains honor, but ruthless men gain only wealth.” Both walk off with something, but it's not the same something. Honor is not something ruthless men get.
Power isn't what Solomon names here. He says, “A gracious woman attains honor…” Honor is what she attains.
Peace is a good thing, but this verse doesn't say it. Solomon says, “A gracious woman attains honor, but ruthless men gain only wealth.” Honor is what she attains.
Yes, the twist! The verse says, “A kind man benefits himself…” Kindness doesn't just go out, it comes back around to the kind man too. Nobody shows kindness to lose.
The verse doesn't mention a master. It says, “A kind man benefits himself, but a cruel man brings trouble on himself.” The kind man himself is the one who benefits.
The king isn't in this verse. Solomon says, “A kind man benefits himself…” The benefit lands on the kind man himself.

That's the word. The verse says, “…but he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward.” Sowing is planting, and what you plant comes up later. The wicked man earns an empty wage, and the one who sows righteousness reaps a true reward.
Hiding doesn't grow anything. Solomon says, “…he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward.” Righteousness has to be sown, not tucked away.
Borrowing is not what Solomon names here. He says, “…he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward.” The one who sows it is the one who reaps.
That's the opposite of what the verse says. Solomon says, “Genuine righteousness leads to life, but the pursuit of evil brings death.” Evil chased all the way ends in death, not life.
Yes, false. The verse says, “Genuine righteousness leads to life, but the pursuit of evil brings death.” Genuine righteousness is the road to life, and the pursuit of evil brings death.
Right. The verse says, “…but the blameless in their walk are His delight.” It's the same word delight as the honest weight back in verse 1. The LORD is glad over those who walk blamelessly.
Giving is a good thing, but this verse names someone else. Solomon says, “…but the blameless in their walk are His delight.” His delight is those whose walk is blameless.
Strength and youth aren't what the verse points at. Solomon says, “…but the blameless in their walk are His delight.” It's about how a person walks, not how strong they are.
That's the word. The verse says, “…but the offspring of the righteous will escape.” The first half says the wicked will not go unpunished. The offspring of the righteous will escape.
Wandering isn't what the verse says. Solomon says, “…but the offspring of the righteous will escape.” They escape.
Ruling is a big promise, and the verse doesn't make it. Solomon says, “…but the offspring of the righteous will escape.” Escape is the word.

explanations.answer: A beautiful woman who lacks discretion
explanations.explanation: Right. The verse says, “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.” Gold is fine, but it looks out of place where it doesn't fit. I think Solomon is saying beauty without discretion sits oddly.

explanations.answer: A rich man who lacks wisdom
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thought, but the verse says something else. Solomon says, “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.” The picture is about a beautiful woman, not a rich man.

explanations.answer: A proud man who lacks humility
explanations.explanation: Pride and humility do show up in this chapter, back in verse 2. But this verse says, “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.” Discretion is the missing piece here.
True. The verse says, “The desire of the righteous leads only to good…” Only good, no side trips. The other half says the hope of the wicked brings wrath.
It's true. Solomon says, “The desire of the righteous leads only to good…” That word only is in the verse. The hope of the wicked brings wrath, but the desire of the righteous leads only to good.
That's what the verse says. “One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor.” Holding back what is right ends in poverty.
Comfortable is not where the verse leaves him. It says the one who withholds what is right does so “…only to become poor.” That only is a plot twist.
Respect isn't in this verse. Solomon says the man who withholds what is right does it “…only to become poor.” Poor is where he ends up.
I get why it sounds likely. Give and give, and you'd think you'd run dry. But Solomon says, “…he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed.” He doesn't end up drained.
Right, it's false. The verse says, “A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed.” The one who refreshes others gets refreshed too.
That's it. The verse says, “The people will curse the hoarder of grain…” The grain is the same either way, but the town knows what the hoarder did. The one who sells it gets a blessing instead.
Thanks goes to the other man. The verse says, “The people will curse the hoarder of grain, but blessing will crown the one who sells it.” Hoarding doesn't earn a thank you.
The people don't let this one slide. Solomon says, “The people will curse the hoarder of grain…” They curse him.
Yes. The verse says, “He who trusts in his riches will fall…” Money makes a wobbly place to stand. Solomon also said riches are worthless in the day of wrath, back in verse 4.
I wish that worked, but the verse says the opposite. Solomon says, “He who trusts in his riches will fall…” Fall is the word.
People might envy him, but the verse never says so. It says, “He who trusts in his riches will fall…” What happens to him is a fall.

True. The verse says, “…but the righteous will thrive like foliage.” Leaves are what a healthy plant shows off, and the righteous thrive in the same way. The man who trusts in his riches falls, and the righteous thrive.
It's true. Solomon says, “…but the righteous will thrive like foliage.” The man trusting in riches falls, and the righteous thrive.

explanations.answer: Servant to the wise of heart
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says, “…and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.” Whoever brings trouble on his house inherits the wind, and the fool ends up serving the wise of heart. That's quite a turn.
He doesn't end up running things. Solomon says, “…the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.” He ends up serving, not ruling.
No field in this verse. Solomon says, “…the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.” Servant is where the fool lands.
That's the one. The verse says, “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise.” The word is wise, not rich or famous.
Rich is not the word here. Solomon says, “…and he who wins souls is wise.” Wise is what he is.
Proud would be a funny way to end that verse, especially after verse 2 said pride is followed by disgrace. But Solomon says, “…and he who wins souls is wise.” Wise is the word.
